article_blocks.text: Strain Type: Indica-dominant hybrid
Genetics: Exceptional phenotype of Skunk #1
Breeder: Exodus Collective in the United Kingdom
THC Content: 16–22%
CBD Content: Usually below 1%
Terpene Profile: Myrcene , beta-caryophyllene , limonene
Primary Flavors: Pungent cheese, Skunk, earth, musk
Flowering Time (Indoor): 7–9 weeks
Outdoor Harvest Time: late September to early October
Indoor Yield: 625–800 g/m²
Outdoor Yield: Up to 800 g per plant
Grow Difficulty: Easy to moderate

Few marijuana strains are as closely connected with the cannabis culture of one country as Cheese is with Britain. Long before dessert strains made food-inspired names commonplace, this unusually pungent plant earned its identity for a simple reason: its flowers produced an aroma that reminded growers of strong, mature cheese. The original Cheese, also known as UK Cheese and later Exodus Cheese , was not created by deliberately crossing two named cultivars. It emerged as an exceptional Skunk #1 phenotype in southern England around the late 1980s and was maintained entirely through cloning. By the mid-1990s, cuttings had reached the Exodus Collective near Luton, whose members freely distributed the plant through the British underground cannabis and free-party communities.

That history makes authentic Cheese fundamentally different from many strains carrying the name today. Seed companies eventually crossed the clone with other marijuana genetics so growers could reproduce Cheese-like plants from seed, but the classic cultivar remains a specific clone-only Skunk #1 selection. Its combination of aggressively savory aroma, strong hybrid effects, heavy production, and relatively short flowering helped transform it from a locally shared cutting into one of the most influential European cannabis varieties of its generation.
Genetics and Lineage

The original Cheese is best documented as a phenotype of Skunk #1. Historical accounts place its discovery around 1988–1989 in the Chiltern area of England, where a grower reportedly started a packet of Skunk #1 and preserved one female because of its exceptionally large flowers and unusual odor. The plant was cloned and eventually became known simply as Cheese. Around 1995, the cutting reached the Exodus Collective near Luton, which played the central role in preserving and distributing it.

That means there is no separate Cheese father or mother to list for the original clone: genetically, it is Skunk #1. Sensi Seeds describes Skunk #1 as a stabilized 65% indica / 35% sativa hybrid built from traditional cannabis populations originating in Afghanistan, Central and South America, and Thailand. Its combination of quick flowering, heavy yields, vigorous branching, and hybrid psychoactivity helps explain many characteristics retained by the Cheese phenotype.

Confusion usually begins with Big Buddha Cheese . In the early 2000s, breeder Milo—better known as Big Buddha—obtained the original Cheese clone and crossed it with a selected Afghani male to create a reproducible seed line. That cultivar became enormously successful and helped spread Cheese genetics internationally, but its lineage is Cheese × Afghani rather than pure Skunk #1. On this page, “Cheese” refers primarily to the classic UK/Exodus clone rather than the later Big Buddha Cheese seed strain.
Effects and Experience

Cheese delivers the kind of hybrid high that helped make old-school Skunk genetics so popular. The onset can feel surprisingly cheerful and mentally energetic for a plant with an indica-dominant background. Mood may rise quickly, conversation can become easier, and ordinary activities can feel more entertaining. Rather than producing an intensely racing cerebral experience, the mental effect usually combines euphoria with a comfortable sense of awareness.

Physical relaxation gradually develops beneath that uplift. Muscles may feel looser and the pace of activity tends to slow, although moderate amounts do not necessarily produce immediate couch-lock. This combination of mental brightness and body relaxation is consistent with the broader Skunk #1 family, which Sensi Seeds describes as combining a creative, long-lasting high with a relaxed stone. Higher doses can push Cheese toward considerably heavier relaxation and eventual drowsiness.

Because the original clone predates modern laboratory testing, there is no authoritative historical THC percentage that defines genuine Cheese. Contemporary material carrying UK Cheese or Exodus Cheese genetics is often reported in roughly the mid-teens through low-20% THC range, although cultivation and selection can move results outside that span. Consumers should rely on the laboratory label of the specific flower rather than assuming that every product sold as Cheese has identical potency.
Medical Benefits

Some medical marijuana consumers have historically favored Cheese because its effects may combine mood elevation with substantial physical relaxation. The more upbeat first stage may appeal to people who prefer cannabis that does not immediately feel sedating, while the heavier portion of the experience can become better suited to quiet evenings and rest. Individual responses, however, vary considerably according to dose, tolerance, cannabinoid chemistry, and consumption method.

Cheese has not been clinically established as a treatment for chronic pain, anxiety, depression, insomnia, or another medical condition. A strain name also cannot reliably predict a therapeutic response because cannabis products sold under the same name may differ chemically. High doses of THC can increase anxiety, dizziness, or cognitive impairment in susceptible consumers. Anyone using marijuana medicinally should consider batch-specific laboratory results, medication interactions, dosage, and professional medical guidance.
Flavor Profile and Aroma

The aroma is the characteristic that made Cheese famous. Instead of the sweeter earth-and-Skunk profile usually associated with Skunk #1, the selected clone developed an intensely pungent, sour, savory smell frequently compared with aged cheese. Breaking apart the flowers can release waves of musk, earth, damp herbs, sharp Skunk, and spice. A subtle fruity or sweet background occasionally appears beneath the heavier funk, but this is not primarily a sugary dessert cultivar.

There is no universal laboratory terpene fingerprint for the original clone. Modern UK Cheese samples and related cultivated material frequently show myrcene, beta-caryophyllene, limonene, humulene, and pinene, but their proportions vary according to environment and phenotype authenticity. The distinctive “cheese” aroma also should not be attributed to a single terpene; cannabis odor is created through a complex mixture of terpenes and other volatile aromatic compounds.

The smoke typically begins earthy, sour, and herbal before developing a creamy or savory quality through the middle. Pepper and Skunk can linger after the exhale, sometimes followed by a faint fruity sweetness. Proper curing is especially important with Cheese because its aggressive aromatic character is the central feature separating the cultivar from ordinary Skunk-derived weed.
Growing Information

The original Cheese clone developed a reputation as a practical production plant as well as an aromatic novelty. Modern nurseries preserving UK Cheese describe it as highly branchy, with strong lateral development and numerous flowering sites instead of relying entirely on one dominant central cola. A typical indoor flowering cycle falls around seven to nine weeks. Prime Cuts Nursery lists approximately 625–800 g/m² indoors and potential outdoor harvests approaching 800 g per plant under favorable conditions, although these figures should be treated as cultivation estimates rather than guarantees.

The cultivar usually responds well to topping and canopy management because its lateral branches naturally create multiple productive sites. Branch support may become useful late in bloom as the flowers gain weight. Its Skunk #1 heritage also contributes vigor and relatively straightforward cultivation; Sensi Seeds describes the underlying Skunk line as robust, strongly branched, quick flowering, and suitable for methods such as SOG , SCROG , supercropping, and lollipopping.

Odor management is one of the more unusual cultivation concerns. Cheese can become intensely aromatic before harvest, making effective ventilation and odor filtration important in indoor environments where smell matters. Outdoor maturity generally arrives from late September into early October for the classic clone under suitable conditions, although weather and latitude affect timing. Dense flowers should be watched carefully during wet autumn conditions, with airflow and plant health taking priority over simply waiting for a calendar date.
FAQ
What are the genetics of Cheese?

The original UK Cheese, also known as Exodus Cheese, is an exceptional clone-only phenotype of Skunk #1. It was selected in England around the late 1980s and later distributed extensively by the Exodus Collective.
Is Cheese the same strain as Exodus Cheese?

In the classic historical sense, yes. Cheese, UK Cheese, and Exodus Cheese are commonly used for the original Skunk #1 clone that became famous through the Exodus Collective. Later seed-bred Cheese varieties may contain additional genetics and are not necessarily identical to that clone.
Is Cheese the same as Big Buddha Cheese?

No. The original Cheese is a Skunk #1 phenotype maintained as a clone. Big Buddha Cheese was created later by crossing that Cheese clone with a selected Afghani male so the genetics could be offered in seed form.
What does the Cheese strain taste like?

The classic profile combines pungent mature-cheese funk with Skunk, earth, herbs, musk, pepper, and occasional fruity sweetness. Its savory aroma is considerably less dessert-like than many modern marijuana strains with food-inspired names.
How long does Cheese take to flower?

The classic UK Cheese clone generally finishes in approximately seven to nine weeks indoors. Outdoor plants typically mature around late September to early October in favorable Northern Hemisphere conditions.
Final Thoughts on Cheese

Cheese occupies an unusual place in cannabis history because its influence began with selection rather than conventional breeding. An anonymous British grower found an extraordinary Skunk #1 female, preserved it as a cutting, and the Exodus Collective later helped spread that clone through the UK. Its smell was so distinctive that a simple nickname became one of the most recognizable strain names in European marijuana culture. The underlying Skunk #1 genetics supplied vigor, short flowering, productivity, and balanced effects; the individual Cheese phenotype supplied an aromatic character unlike the rest of the population.

Later breeders transformed that clone into an entire family. Big Buddha’s Cheese × Afghani work brought the profile into seed form, while countless subsequent hybrids added Blueberry , Haze , Kush , and other genetics to the Cheese foundation. None of those descendants changes the identity of the original: classic Cheese is the clone-only Skunk #1 phenotype associated with the British Exodus scene. Its combination of savory funk, euphoric hybrid effects, strong yields, and unmistakable cultural history makes it more than another old-school strain—it remains one of the cultivars that gave British cannabis its own internationally recognized genetic identity.
